tip: 'Di-' flips who acts: 'ditawar' = get bargained; 'harganya boleh ditawar' = the price can be haggled.
In casual speech, 'ke-…-an' can mean 'too X': 'mahal' → 'kemahalan' = too expensive, overpriced.
The suffix '-kan' often means 'cause to': 'turun' = go down, 'turunkan' = lower it. 'Turunkan harganya!'
'Harga pas' = fixed price – the seller's polite signal that bargaining is over.
'Ya sudah' = alright then – the giving-in phrase: 'Ya sudah, dua ratus ribu saja'.
'Menawar' = to haggle; 'menawarkan' = to offer. 'Saya menawar harganya' = I bargained over the price.
'QRIS' (say: kris) is the QR code payment used almost everywhere: 'bayar pakai QRIS'.
Put the thing first for done deals: 'uangnya sudah saya transfer' = the money, I already sent.
'Nota' = the handwritten receipt from small shops; 'struk' = the printed one.
'Kembalian' = your change, from 'kembali' (come back): 'Ini kembaliannya'.
'Mbak' politely addresses a young woman: 'Maaf, Mbak' = excuse me, miss.
The ending '-nya' often works like 'the': 'kembalian' = change, 'kembaliannya' = the change we both know about. 'Simpan kembaliannya' = keep the change.
'Ter-' often means 'by accident': 'tertelan' = got swallowed. 'Kartu ATM saya tertelan'.
'Tinggal' usually means 'live', but with amounts it means what's left: 'saldo saya tinggal dua ratus ribu' = my balance is down to 200,000.
'Habis' = used up, and it stands alone as the whole statement: 'pulsa saya habis' = my credit ran out. No extra verb needed.
'Isikan' = fill it for someone: 'isikan pulsa ke nomor ini' = top up this number.
'Kilat' = lightning: 'pos kilat' = express mail. 'Kalau pakai kilat' = if you use express.
Pending things take 'belum', not 'tidak': 'belum sampai' = hasn't arrived yet. 'Tidak sampai' would mean it's not coming at all – 'belum' says you still expect it.
'Boleh' asks permission, 'bisa' is ability. 'Boleh saya pinjam uang?' = may I borrow money? Use 'boleh' when you need a yes from someone.
'Meminjam' = borrow, 'meminjamkan' = lend: 'meminjamkan uang ke saya' = lent money to me.
'Struknya mau dibawa?' is the stock checkout question – cashiers ask it at nearly every register; 'struk' = receipt. Answer 'Mau' (yes please) or 'Tidak usah' (no need).
'Lumayan' = not bad, pretty good – the word for pleasant surprises: 'Diskonnya lumayan!'
Indonesians usually just say 'money changer'; 'tempat penukaran uang' is the formal sign version.
'Titip' = ask someone to bring or get something: 'Titip beli sabun, ya' = please get me soap.
For meetings, 'mundur' = pushed later: 'rapat mundur satu jam' = the meeting moved back an hour.
'Maju' means go forward, and on a schedule forward = earlier: 'rapat maju jadi jam delapan' = the meeting moved up to eight. The opposite, postponed, is 'diundur'.
'Di-' = done to it: 'diundur' = postponed (by someone) – 'rapat diundur ke minggu depan'.
Formal: use the title instead of 'kamu' – 'apakah Bapak bisa hadir?' = can you attend, sir?
Office speech uses 'deadline'; 'tenggat' is its formal written synonym.
'Paling lambat besok siang' = by tomorrow noon at the latest. Its partner is 'paling cepat' (at the earliest) – the pair brackets any deadline window.
